name: Fu Manchu moustache

card.summary: A long, straight moustache that grows from the lip corners and hangs down past the mouth or chin, worn as a bold facial-hair style that frames the lower face.
card.note: Named after a fictional character and associated with ethnic caricature; also slow and demanding to grow and maintain.

quick.overview:
The Fu Manchu is a moustache that grows straight from the corners of the upper lip and hangs downward in two tapered tendrils, often past the jawline. Some versions add a third tendril from a chin patch.

People wear it as a distinctive style that draws the eye down the lower face and elongates it. It is a competition category at moustache championships. The name comes from the fictional villain Fu Manchu, and the style has been criticized for its link to stereotyping of East Asians.
quick.how: It requires growing hair from the lip corners only, so growth is slower and sparser than for a horseshoe moustache. Wearers keep the cheeks and chin shaved, trim, comb and condition the hair and may use a little wax to train it downward.
quick.risks: There are no health risks beyond ordinary skin irritation from shaving and grooming. Socially, the style carries historical associations with caricature, and results depend on genetics and density of moustache hair.

lead: The Fu Manchu moustache is a full, straight moustache that extends past the corners of the mouth and hangs down in two tapered tendrils, often past the jawline.[1] Some versions add a third tendril from a chin patch.[1]

People wear it as a stylized facial-hair look. Because it grows only from the corners of the upper lip, it is harder and slower to grow than a horseshoe moustache, and it is a competition category at the World Beard and Moustache Championships.[1] It is often confused with the horseshoe moustache, which also includes hair at the sides of the lips and chin and does not hang over the jaw.[1]

The name derives from the fictional villain Fu Manchu, created by Sax Rohmer. The book character has no moustache; the look came from film adaptations, first appearing in the 1929 British serial The Mystery of Dr. Fu Manchu, and then became a staple for screen villains, with Christopher Lee wearing it in The Face of Fu Manchu (1965).[1] The style became visual shorthand for villainous East Asian characters and was used to stereotype Chinese people, which is the main criticism of it.[1]

angle.text: The moustache adds length and a downward frame to the lower face. It is chosen as a bold style statement, and its look depends on the density of moustache hair.

paras: The Fu Manchu is a straight moustache with ends that point downward, generally extending beyond the chin.[2] Grooming guidance summarized by Grokipedia describes keeping the cheeks, chin and the groove below the nose shaved, trimming weekly, combing the ends to hang down, and using wax and beard oil.[3]

Grokipedia's account says drooping moustaches were worn by elite men in Qing dynasty China as signs of maturity and authority, before the Western caricature was created.[3] That account is AI-generated and should be read with caution. Wikipedia places the origin of the name in the Fu Manchu film adaptations of the early twentieth century.[1]

Wikipedia notes the moustache became a visual shorthand for villainous East Asian characters and was used in caricatures of Chinese people in the 19th and early 20th centuries.[1] The broader history of moustaches runs from Ancient Egypt to the 1880s-1890s Western peak and a revival in the 1960s.[2]

timeline.event: The Mystery of Dr. Fu Manchu serial introduces the look on screen.[1]
Christopher Lee wears it in The Face of Fu Manchu.[1]
